doc.title: Jackie McLean — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Current playing, teaching and Dizzy Gillespie
title: Ear versus paper, and giving students a concept
summary: McLean is 98% an ear musician; he develops students' concept by playing them the records that first woke him, from Lester Young to Eckstine, Monk, Dameron and Bird.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You mentioned – in that sound, where – how much are you an ear musician versus a paper musician?
I’m 98% an ear musician and 2% a paper musician.
What do you think? Is that a function – well, it’s a function of how you developed. But, in developing musicians, where do you place the emphasis?

I’m fortunate that I have people on my staff that can cover all the bases. So if they come with me, they come to – what I call, to develop a concept. That’s what I give them. I help develop their concept by letting them experience what I experienced, what I heard, what I listened to, and what made me begin to develop. I bring it to them. Same recordings, same stuff. All the recordings that I first listened to, from the first one, which was Just You, Just Me, with Lester Young, Johnny Guarnieri, Sid Catlett, and Slam Stewart. I say, “Listen to this. This is what I first heard. It gave me a wakeup call.” I take them through that piece and bring out to them what I – what excited me about the recording, so they can begin to visualize some of the things that I had. And take them through the Billy Eckstine big bands, through Thelonious’s music, and Tadd’s music [Tadd Dameron], that whole period. Of course Bird, Sonny Stitt. I just try to help them develop a concept that will be really hip and together.
